---
title: "random forests"
---

## intuition

- a single [decision tree](decision-trees.qmd) memorises training data — low bias, high variance. the fix: train many trees on randomised versions of the data and features, then average their predictions
- two sources of randomness decorrelate the trees:
  1. **bagging** (bootstrap aggregating) — each tree trains on a bootstrap sample: $n$ rows drawn with replacement from the training set
  2. **feature randomness** — at each split, only a random subset of features is considered, not all of them

## bootstrap sampling & out-of-bag error

- sampling with replacement means a bootstrap sample of size $n$ drawn from $n$ points contains, on average, about 63.2% of the unique original points; the remaining $\approx$36.8%, never selected for that tree, form its **out-of-bag (oob)** set
- each tree's oob set works like a built-in validation set for that tree — averaging oob error across all trees gives a performance estimate without a separate held-out split, see [train/test splits](../training-evaluation/train-test.qmd)

## why averaging reduces variance

- if each tree has variance $\sigma^2$ and the trees are perfectly correlated ($\rho=1$), averaging them changes nothing — the ensemble has the same variance as a single tree
- if the trees are decorrelated ($\rho<1$), the ensemble's variance is $\operatorname{var}(\text{avg})=\rho\sigma^2+\dfrac{(1-\rho)\sigma^2}{b}$ for $b$ trees — as $b\to\infty$ this approaches $\rho\sigma^2$, strictly less than a single tree's variance
- feature randomness is what keeps $\rho$ low: without it, every tree would tend to split on the same dominant features first and end up highly correlated, capping how much averaging can help — this is the core trick behind random forests

## key hyperparameters

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| hyperparameter | controls | typical guidance |
|---|---|---|
| `n_estimators` (number of trees, $b$) | ensemble size | more trees reduce variance with diminishing returns; rarely overfits by itself |
| `max_features` | size of the random feature subset considered at each split | $\sqrt p$ for classification, $p/3$ for regression are common defaults |
| `max_depth` | depth of each individual tree | deeper trees fit more per tree, raising that tree's variance — offset by averaging across trees |
| `min_samples_leaf` | minimum points per leaf | larger values smooth predictions and reduce overfitting of individual trees |

:::

## prediction

- regression: average the predictions across all $b$ trees
- classification: majority vote across trees, or average each tree's predicted class probabilities

## practical considerations

- random forests are a strong, low-effort baseline — they rarely overfit badly even with many trees and default settings, unlike a single deep tree left unchecked, see [bias-variance tradeoff](../training-evaluation/bias-variance.qmd)
- feature importance (e.g. mean decrease in impurity) is a common output, but impurity-based importance is biased toward high-cardinality features; permutation importance is more reliable, see [correlation & statistical tests](../training-evaluation/statistical-tests.qmd) for other ways to screen features
- **shap** (shapley additive explanations) goes further: instead of one importance score per feature for the whole model, it gives a per-prediction, per-feature contribution, grounded in game-theoretic shapley values — useful when the question is "why did the model flag *this* patient," not just "which features matter on average" [shap documentation](https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)
- shap values are additive — they sum to the difference between a prediction and the model's average output — which is what makes individual-prediction explanations like "feature x pushed this patient's risk score up by 0.12" meaningful; plain feature importance can't make that kind of statement
- random forests train trees independently and in parallel, unlike [gradient boosting](gradient-boosting.qmd), which fits trees sequentially — easier to parallelise, but generally needs more trees to match boosting's accuracy at a comparable budget
